Have you ever filed your tax return?

You visit a tax office. The tax officer looks at what you have a salary, a rental property, a business and calculates tax differently for each one. You do not change what you are. The officer just applies different rules depending on what they are visiting.

Next year a new officer comes in an auditor. Same objects salary, property, business but completely different operations. You still do not change anything. The auditor just visits and does their own thing.
This is exactly what the Visitor Pattern does.
Without the pattern:
Every new operation audit, report, export means cracking open every single class and adding a new method. Ten classes times five operations equals fifty methods scattered everywhere.
With Visitor:
Each operation lives in its own visitor class. Add a new operation create one new visitor. Zero changes to existing classes.
It is useful when:

["You have a fixed set of classes but need to add new operations frequently.","You want to keep unrelated behaviors out of your domain classes.","You want to avoid instanceof chains to figure out what type you are dealing with."]
items: You have a fixed set of classes but need to add new operations frequently.
You want to keep unrelated behaviors out of your domain classes.
You want to avoid instanceof chains to figure out what type you are dealing with.

1. The Problem: Adding Operations to a Shopping Cart

Each item needs to support multiple operations:

The simplest approach is to add all these methods to each item class:

blocks.content: Why This Breaks Down

1. Violates Single Responsibility Each item class now contains tax logic, discount logic, invoice logic, and delivery logic all completely unrelated to what an item actually is. The classes are bloated and hard to maintain.

2. Hard to Extend Need a new operation like exportToAccountingSoftware() or calculateShippingWeight()? You must open every single item class and add the method. Three classes today, ten classes tomorrow the problem compounds fast. This violates the Open/Closed Principle.
3. You Don't Always Control the Classes What if item classes come from a third-party library or are auto-generated? You cannot add methods directly.

4. Scattered Logic Tax calculation logic for all item types is spread across three different classes. To understand how tax works, you have to jump between files. Changing the tax rules means hunting through every class.
What We Really Need

["Keep item classes clean they should only know what they are, not what can be done with them.","Add new operations without modifying existing item classes.","Keep all logic for one operation tax, discount, invoice in one place."]
items: Keep item classes clean they should only know what they are, not what can be done with them.
Add new operations without modifying existing item classes.
Keep all logic for one operation tax, discount, invoice in one place.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Visitor Pattern is designed to solve.
2. What is the Visitor Pattern?
The Visitor Pattern lets you separate algorithms from the objects they operate on. It enables you to add new operations to a class hierarchy without modifying the classes themselves.
Two characteristics define it:

1. Separation of algorithm and structure The item classes stay clean they only hold their data. All operational logic lives in separate visitor classes. Tax logic lives in TaxVisitor. Discount logic lives in DiscountVisitor. Each operation is completely isolated.

2. Double dispatch The correct method to call is determined by both the type of the element and the type of the visitor. The element calls back the visitor with this which tells the visitor exactly what concrete type it is dealing with. This two-step dispatch eliminates all instanceof checks.

Real-World Analogy

Think about a shopping mall inspection.

The mall has different types of stores a food court, a clothing shop, an electronics store. Different inspectors visit the mall a health inspector, a fire safety officer, an electrical auditor. Each inspector visits every store and applies their own rules.

The stores do not need to know how to evaluate their own fire safety or electrical wiring. They just open the door and let each inspector do their job. Adding a new type of inspection say a noise compliance audit does not require changing any store. You just bring in a new inspector.

The Visitor Pattern works the same way elements accept visitors, and new operations are just new visitors.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: Class Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245816711-0f33791d.png
The Four Participants

Element Interface CartItem Declares only accept(ItemVisitor) plus basic getters. No operation logic anywhere. The accept()method is the entry point for double dispatch each element calls back the visitor with this, telling it exactly which concrete type it is dealing with.

Concrete Elements PhysicalItem, DigitalItem, SubscriptionItem Each implements accept() by calling the correct visitor method  visitor.visitPhysical(this), visitor.visitDigital(this), visitor.visitSubscription(this). That one line is all the pattern needs from the element side.

Visitor Interface ItemVisitor Declares a visit method for every concrete element type. Every new operation implements this interface. The compiler enforces that every visitor handles every element type.

Concrete Visitors TaxVisitor, DiscountVisitor, InvoiceVisitor Each implements one complete operation across all item types. All tax logic lives in TaxVisitor. All discount logic lives in DiscountVisitor. Add a new operation create one new visitor class, zero changes to items.
3. How It Works
The Visitor workflow involves a two-step dispatch that routes execution to the right method based on both the element type and the visitor type.
Sequence Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245817029-4d845d74.png
Step 1 The client creates a concrete visitor TaxVisitor, DiscountVisitor, or InvoiceVisitor.
Step 2 The client iterates over the cart items and calls item.accept(visitor) on each one.

Step 3 Inside accept() each element calls back the visitor's specific method visitor.visitPhysical(this) for a PhysicalItem, visitor.visitDigital(this) for a DigitalItem. This is the double dispatch the element resolves its own concrete type.
Step 4 The visitor's visitPhysical() or visitDigital() method runs and performs the operation using the element's own data.
Step 5 To add a new operation say DeliveryEstimateVisitor you create one new visitor class. Zero element classes change.
